result.rationale: Both plans are competent and match the goal (blind identification of anonymized IDs). The decisive question is which controls the error the PM says kills the work: a confident wrong match. Plan B is built exactly around that. Its register split (A=panel inputs, B=anchors used for scoring only, CI failing if an anchor leaks into features) directly prevents the circularity where the thing you're trying to predict quietly informs the fingerprint. Its holdout unit is the institution (leave-one-institution-out, then leave-one-country-out), which is the correct unit when the claim is 'we can identify institutions we haven't seen labeled.' It pre-commits a precision target (95%) with an abstain sink and calibrated thresholds (Venn-Abers/conformal), so the default is UNKNOWN rather than a forced guess — the right posture when Type I is ruinous. It sequences a kill pilot first (Netherlands; if it fails there, stop) and puts negative controls (permuted fingerprints score at chance, phantom IDs must abstain) at the front. For a desk that will size real positions on a specific bank's customers, 'these clusters are stable' is not the evidence the PM asked for; 'here is held-out precision on institutions labeled from an independent survey' is. Plan A confronts this head-on as its framing premise and defends against it with a realized-LTM-EBITDA denominator (denominator not estimated), a feasibility gate (H0) that can kill the study in week one, and same-analyst-set revision measurement from detail files rather than the summary tape. Plan B acknowledges the same mechanical problem but keeps NTM EBITDA in the denominator and relies on an ex-post identity decomposition and 'report with/without Delta NTM EBITDA control' to disentangle it — a weaker fix that leaves the headline exposed to exactly the contamination the question warns about. Plan A also sequences the kill test first (H0 feasibility gate, then first-stage beta threshold with a stop), which is the right entropy-reducing order and gives the fund a cheap early exit. On economics, Plan B asserts specific elasticity magnitudes (8-12%/100bp, 2-5% measured) up front as anchors; Plan A derives beta* from realized persistence rather than importing a number. Plan A's main costs are real: it is heavy, imports a TAQ reverse-causality check the firm has no tick data to run (a firm-fit slip), and its regime-instability machinery (Bai-Perron, Kalman, variance ratios) is more than a 6-18mo fundamental shop can inspect or defend to a PM. Plan B is more restrained and its practical quintile-sort out-of-sample validation is exactly the judgeable output this fund can use. But measurement validity on the core circularity dominates: a cleaner-measured true effect beats a contaminated one wrapped in a good validation grid.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A answers the question actually asked — do CAGR revisions drive peer-relative re-rating — with a design this firm can run and defend, while Plan B silently swaps the question for regime-instability and market-efficiency tests and reaches for infrastructure (TAQ, block bootstrap, Bai-Perron, Kalman) this fund cannot staff or evaluate.

A is the plan that answers this question for this firm.
